> Simon Ayotte, Principal Scientist – Lasers and Photonics, indie’s Photonics BU


The demand for increasingly precise timing and frequency references continues to grow across scientific, industrial, and defense applications. Modern communications networks, quantum technologies, precision sensing systems, GPS free inertial navigation, and time-distribution infrastructure all depend on stable and accurately controlled frequency sources.


## Introduction


For decades, the highest levels of timing performance were achieved using microwave-based references such as quartz oscillators, rubidium standards, cesium clocks, and hydrogen masers. While these technologies remain essential, advances in laser physics and photonics have enabled a transition toward optical frequency references operating at frequencies that are thousands of times higher than conventional microwave standards. Because optical frequencies are much higher, a given fractional frequency error corresponds to a much smaller interval of time, enabling clocks and timing systems with significantly improved stability, accuracy, and phase-noise performance.


At its core, a clock measures time by counting the cycles of a highly stable oscillator. In a quartz clock, this oscillator is a vibrating crystal. In an optical clock, it is a laser stabilized to an atomic or molecular transition, producing an exceptionally stable optical frequency reference. A clock can therefore be viewed as a stable oscillator combined with a counter. The challenge is that optical frequencies are hundreds of thousands of times higher than those used in conventional electronic clocks and cannot be counted directly by digital electronics. A frequency comb provides the link between the optical and electronic worlds by translating the stability of the optical reference into usable optical and RF signals that can be counted electronically to generate a time scale. Optical clocks and frequency combs therefore play complementary roles. The optical clock generates the stable optical reference, while the frequency comb transfers that stability into practical timing and frequency signals. Together, they enable timing systems with unprecedented stability, accuracy, and phase-noise performance1 .


The simplified architecture of such a system is shown in Figure 1 from the laser up to the clock time scale output. An optical clock does not directly produce a “1 second tick”. It produces an extremely stable RF frequency. Time is obtained by counting cycles of that frequency.


While atomic or molecular references define the ultimate accuracy of an optical clock, the clock’s performance depends critically on the quality of its laser source. Laser linewidth and frequency noise directly influence the ability to interrogate the reference and capture its stability. Recent advances in semiconductor laser technology have made it possible to achieve ultra-narrow linewidths in compact and robust architectures, significantly reducing size, weight, and power (SWaP) compared with traditional solutions.


This application note introduces the fundamental building blocks of optical timing systems and highlights the role of ultra-narrow-linewidth semiconductor lasers in next-generation optical clocks.


## How an Optical Clock Generates Time and Frequency Signals


Figure 1 illustrates the simplified architecture of an optical timing system. A narrow-linewidth laser is stabilized to a frequency reference, creating an exceptionally stable optical frequency. This optical signal can be used directly as an optical frequency reference, or transferred to an optical frequency comb. The frequency comb acts as a bridge between optical and electronic frequencies. When the comb pulse train is detected on a photodetector, it generates RF signals at the comb repetition frequency (frep) and its harmonics (2frep, 3frep, …). These RF signals inherit the stability of the optical reference while remaining accessible to conventional electronic instruments. A selected RF component can then be filtered, amplified, and counted electronically to generate a practical time scale. At the same time, the comb provides access to thousands of phase-coherent optical frequencies spanning a broad wavelength range, enabling optical frequency synthesis.


Figure 1. Simplified optical timing architecture. A narrow-linewidth laser is stabilized to a frequency reference using a feedback loop, creating a highly stable optical frequency reference. This optical signal can be used directly as a continuous-wave (CW) frequency reference, transferred to an optical frequency comb for optical frequency synthesis, or converted into a low-noise RF reference through optical frequency division. A time scale is generated by electronically counting cycles of the RF reference.


Although optical timing systems can vary significantly in complexity, most are built around three fundamental elements: a frequency reference, a narrow-linewidth laser, and a frequency comb. Together, they enable the generation, distribution, and synthesis of highly stable optical and RF frequencies.


### Frequency Reference


Every clock requires a reference that defines a frequency with high stability and repeatability. Depending on the application, the reference may be molecular, atomic, or cavity based. In state-of-the-art systems, atoms are laser-cooled and trapped to suppress motion-induced shifts, while less precise clocks may use thermal atoms or atomic beams.


### Narrow-Linewidth Laser


The laser serves as the optical oscillator that interacts with the reference. Its role is to faithfully transfer the stability of the atomic or molecular transition into a usable optical signal. Key laser characteristics include:


- Narrow linewidth and low phase noise
- Long coherence length
- Low drift
- Fast frequency actuation and high tuning bandwidth


Even when a highly stable atomic or molecular reference is available, the laser remains a critical part of the system. The reference can only correct frequency fluctuations that fall within the bandwidth and dynamic range of the stabilization loops. If the free-running laser exhibits excessive frequency noise, linewidth, or drift, the locking system may be unable to fully suppress these fluctuations. Similarly, insufficient laser tuning bandwidth can limit servo-loop gain and bandwidth, reducing the amount of reference stability that can be transferred to the optical signal. As a result, achievable clock performance depends not only on the quality of the reference itself, but also on the noise characteristics and frequency control capabilities of the laser. In many optical clock and frequency-comb architectures, the laser becomes one of the primary determinants of achievable stability.


### Frequency Comb


A frequency comb acts as a coherent bridge between optical and microwave frequencies. It generates thousands to millions of equally spaced optical lines, often referred to as comb teeth, whose frequencies are described by:


fn=nfrep+fCEOf_{n} = nf_{rep} + f_{CEO}


- fn is the frequency of a comb tooth,
- frep is the repetition frequency of the comb,
- fCEO is the carrier-envelope offset frequency


Together, frep and fCEO determine the absolute frequency of every comb tooth. To establish a precise link between optical and RF frequencies, both frep and fCEO must be controlled.


In a self-referenced octave-spanning comb, fCEO can be measured using f-to-2f interferometry. A comb tooth at frequency fn is frequency doubled and compared with a tooth one octave higher (f2n), yielding:


fCEO=2fn−f2nf_{CEO} = 2f_{n} – f_{2n}


The octave-spanning spectrum is therefore essential because it enables direct measurement and stabilization of fCEO.


The comb is then referenced to the stabilized CW laser by comparing a comb tooth with the optical reference and generating a beat signal. A feedback loop acts on frep to maintain a constant frequency relationship between the comb tooth and the laser. Once fCEO is stabilized and one comb tooth is referenced to the laser, the frequencies of all comb teeth become known and phase-coherent with the optical reference.


When detected on a photodetector, the comb pulse train generates RF signals at the repetition frequency and its harmonics:


frep,2frep,3frep,…f_{rep}, 2f_{rep}, 3f_{rep},…


A selected RF component can then be filtered, amplified, and used as a highly stable frequency reference. Because the comb transfers the stability of the optical reference to frep, the exceptional stability of an optical clock can be converted into ultra-low-noise RF and microwave signals. This process is known as optical frequency division.


In addition to generating RF references, the comb provides access to thousands of phase-coherent optical frequencies spanning a broad wavelength range. Once frep and fCEO are stabilized, every comb tooth is known and phase-coherent with the optical reference, enabling optical frequency synthesis across a wide spectral range.


In this sense, the frequency comb transforms a stable optical reference into a practical timing system capable of generating both optical and RF frequency references.


Figure 2. Self-referenced octave-spanning optical frequency comb. The octave-spanning spectrum enables measurement and stabilization of the carrier-envelope offset frequency (fCEO) through f-to-2f interferometry. A comb tooth is referenced to the stabilized CW laser, while a feedback loop acting on frep transfers the stability of the optical reference to the entire comb. Detection of the comb pulse train on a photodetector generates RF signals at frep and its harmonics, enabling optical frequency division and precision timing.


### Key Takeaway


While atomic and molecular transitions provide the ultimate reference, optical timing performance depends on the successful interaction of all three building blocks: a stable reference, a narrow-linewidth laser, and a frequency comb. Together they enable the generation of optical and microwave signals with levels of stability that would be difficult or impossible to achieve using conventional RF technologies alone.


## Choosing the Right Frequency Reference


The frequency reference is often the single most important design choice in an optical timing system. It determines not only the achievable stability and accuracy, but also the system complexity, SWaP, and implementation cost. Depending on the application, an optical cavity, a molecular reference or an atomic reference, may provide the best solution. The following sections compare these approaches and highlight the trade-offs between performance and complexity.


### Optical Cavities


In some systems, an ultra-stable optical cavity provides exceptional short-term stability2 . These systems are often used as optical flywheel oscillators and can serve as intermediate references in advance timing architectures.


### Molecularly Referenced Systems


Molecular absorption lines provide a practical and compact approach to generating stable optical frequency references. Common examples include acetylene (C2H2) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN), which offer well characterized transitions in the near-infrared region3 .


Molecular references differ primarily by the nature of the frequency reference itself rather than by the overall system architecture. As described in Section 2, a stabilized laser and frequency comb can still be used; however, the laser is locked to a molecular transition rather than an atomic transition or optical cavity.


Compared with atomic clock architectures, molecular references offer several advantages:


- Compact implementation
- No vacuum chamber required
- No laser cooling or atom trapping
- Mature component ecosystem
- Excellent stability for many sensing and timing applications


Although molecular transitions are generally broader than optical atomic clock transitions, they provide sufficient stability for many practical applications, including coherent sensing, optical frequency transfers, low-phase-noise microwave generation, frequency-comb stabilization, and timing distribution networks.


### Atomically Referenced Systems


Atomic references provide access to highly reproducible frequency standards and form the foundation of modern optical clocks4 . Compared with molecular references, atomic transitions can offer significantly higher stability and accuracy, enabling timing systems that range from compact vapor-cell references to state-of-the-art optical clocks. Examples include: Rubidium (Rb), Potassium (K), Ytterbium (Yb) and Strontium (Sr).


One attractive example is the rubidium two-photon transition at 778.1 nm, which can be accessed by frequency doubling a laser operating near 1556.2 nm. This approach provides the benefits of an atomic reference while avoiding much of the complexity associated with optical clocks. At the other end of the spectrum, atomic clocks based on ytterbium and strontium rely on laser cooling, optical trapping, and multiple stabilized lasers to interrogate extremely narrow atomic transitions.


The complexity of these systems is justified by their exceptional performance. While molecular and alkaliatom references typically exhibit spectroscopic features in the MHz regime, optical clock transitions in ytterbium and strontium can exhibit linewidths in the Hz to sub-Hz regime. Such narrow resonances make it possible to detect and correct extremely small frequency errors, enabling levels of stability and accuracy unattainable with broader resonances.


As the reference transition becomes narrower, the requirements imposed on the laser become increasingly demanding. Fully exploiting advanced atomic references requires lasers with exceptionally low frequency noise, narrow linewidth, and the ability to support highperformance stabilization loops.


### Examples of Atomic Reference Platforms


Plateform Typical Complexity Typical Laser Count Typical SWaP Primary Applications


Rb vapor cell Low 1 Low Frequency references, timing, sensing


Rb two-photon reference Low-Medium 1 Low-Medium Precision frequency references, synchronization


Yb optical clock High 3-5 High Optical clocks, quantum sensing


SR optical clock Very High 4-8 Very High Precision metrology, state-of-the-art optical clocks


This progression illustrates the trade-offs between implementation complexity, SWaP, and ultimate clock performance.


### Reference Linewidth and System Requirements


The achievable performance of a timing system is closely related to the width of the reference transition used for stabilization.


Reference Type Typical Effective Transition Width


Molecular references (C2H2, HCN) MHz regime


Alkali atomic references (Rb vapor cell, Rb two-photon) MHz to sub-MHz regime


Optical clock transitions (Yb, Sr) Hz to sub-Hz regime


As transition linewidth decreases, smaller frequency errors can be detected and corrected. Narrower references can therefore support higher stability and accuracy, but they also impose stricter requirements on the laser used to interrogate them. Consequently, advanced optical timing systems increasingly rely on lasers that combine:


- Ultra-low frequency noise and narrow linewidth
- Fast frequency tuning capability
- High stabilization bandwidth


### Key Takeaway


Atomic references span a broad range of complexity, from compact rubidium-based systems to state-of-the-art atomic clocks. As reference transitions become narrower and more precise, laser performance becomes increasingly critical for capturing, stabilizing, and transferring the information contained in those references.


## Extending Access Through Wavelength Conversion


Many molecular and atomic references lie outside the native wavelength range of a practical laser source. Nonlinear wavelength conversion provides an elegant solution, allowing a single narrow-linewidth infrared laser platform to access a wide range of transitions while preserving frequency stability and coherence. With wavelength coverage spanning 1510-1590 nm, a common laser platform can provide:


- Direct access: 1510-1590 nm
- Second Harmonic Generation (SHG): 755-795 nm
- Third Harmonic Generation (THG): 503-530 nm
- Fourth Harmonic Generation (FHG): 378-397 nm


### Direct Access to Molecular References


The 1510-1590 nm wavelength range provides direct access to important molecular references such as acetylene (C2H2) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN). These references are widely used for frequency stabilization, frequency-comb systems, spectroscopy, and optical frequency division, while avoiding the complexity of vacuum systems and laser cooling.


### Accessing Atomic References Through Frequency Doubling


Second-harmonic generation extends infrared laser platforms into wavelength regions commonly used for atomic references. A particularly attractive example is the rubidium two-photon transition at 778.1 nm, which can be reached by frequency doubling a 1556.2 nm laser:


1556.2 nm Laser → Frequency Doubler → 778.1 nm Radiation → Rb Vapor Cell → Frequency Lock


Unlike many optical clock architectures, the rubidium two-photon reference can be implemented using a simple vapor cell and does not require laser cooling, optical trapping, or ultra-high-vacuum systems. A notable real-world example is a master laser designed and manufactured by indie, operating at 1556.2 nm and stabilized to the rubidium two-photon transition through second-harmonic generation. This system has been deployed as a frequency reference for synchronization of the ALMA radio telescope array in Chile, demonstrating the practicality of combining atomic referencing with nonlinear wavelength conversion.


Figure 3. ALMA radiotelescope antennae synchronized by a master laser and slave lasers. The master laser is a 1556.2 nm laser stabilized to the Rb two-photon transition5 .


Second-harmonic generation also provides access to the rubidium D2 transition at 780.2 nm and several potassium transitions used in atomic physics, laser cooling, sensing, and frequency-reference applications.


### Examples of References Accessible with 1510-1590 nm Lasers

### Key Takeaway


Through direct access and nonlinear wavelength conversion, a single narrow-linewidth infrared laser platform can support molecular references, atomic references, frequency comb stabilization, and precision timing applications. This flexibility enables a common laser technology to address a broad range of current and emerging optical timing architectures.


## The Laser: A key Limitation for Precision in Optical Clocks


A frequency reference alone does not create a practical clock. Whether the reference is molecular, atomic, or cavity based, its stability must first be captured by a laser and then transferred to a frequency comb and, ultimately, to a timing output. As a result, the performance of an optical timing system depends not only on the quality of the reference, but also on the characteristics of the laser used to interrogate and stabilize to that reference.


### Resolving the Reference


The laser must be sufficiently stable to resolve the spectral feature being used as a reference. Excessive frequency noise broadens the observed resonance, degrades lock quality, and limits the achievable stability of the system. This becomes increasingly important as timing architectures move from molecular references toward narrower atomic transitions and more demanding frequency-comb systems. The benefit of a highly stable reference can only be realized if the laser is capable of faithfully tracking it.


In practical terms, lower laser frequency noise enables:


- More stable reference locks
- Higher signal-to-noise ratio
- Improved frequency-comb stabilization
- Lower phase-noise RF generation
- Better overall timing performance


### Locking Bandwidth Matters


Laser stability alone is not sufficient. The laser must also respond rapidly to correction signals generated by the stabilization electronics. The achievable lock performance depends on the bandwidth and gain of the control loop. Higher servo bandwidth allows faster correction of frequency fluctuations, while higher loop gain improves suppression of residual noise. This places an important requirement on the laser source: it must provide a fast and efficient frequency tuning mechanism.


A laser with limited tuning bandwidth can restrict servo performance and prevent the stabilization system from fully exploiting the quality of the reference. Conversely, a laser that supports high-speed frequency actuation enables tighter locks, improved noise suppression, and more effective transfer of reference stability into the optical and RF domains.


### Transferring Stability Through the Frequency Comb


Once stabilized, the laser acts as the bridge between the reference and the frequency comb. The comb does not create stability; it transfers stability. Any residual laser frequency noise can propagate through the comb and ultimately appear as excess phase noise on the generated microwave or timing signal.


For this reason, optical clocks, frequency-comb systems, and optical frequency division architectures share a common set of laser requirements:


- Ultra-low frequency noise & Narrow linewidth
- Fast frequency actuation & High locking bandwidth
capability
- Compact and robust implementation


As optical timing technologies continue to move beyond research laboratories and into deployable systems, these attributes become increasingly important.

## Outlook: Toward Compact Optical Clock and Frequency Comb Systems


The long-term trend in optical timing is clear: systems that once occupied entire optical tables are steadily evolving toward solutions with lower SWaP, improved robustness, and greater deployability. Frequency combs, photonic integration, and semiconductor laser technologies are enabling a transition from laboratory-scale instruments toward compact optical timing systems suitable for real-world applications. As this evolution continues, the ability to generate ultra-stable optical frequencies in a compact form factor will become increasingly important.


The LXM-U platform demonstrates how this can be achieved. By combining a semiconductor laser with an internal frequency reference and a high-bandwidth stabilization loop, linewidths down to 10 Hz can be achieved within a compact and robust architecture. This approach provides the coherence required for demanding applications such as molecular and atomic references, frequency-comb stabilization, optical frequency division, and precision synchronization.


Looking ahead, the same stabilization architecture can be extended beyond infrared wavelengths. Visible semiconductor lasers integrated within an LXM-U-type platform could directly access atomic and quantum transitions while benefiting from the same combination of internal referencing, high-bandwidth frequency control, and ultra-low frequency noise. Such an approach has the potential to simplify future atomic references, quantum sensors, and compact optical clock systems by reducing dependence on larger bulk-optic laser architectures.


As optical clocks and frequency combs continue their transition from the laboratory to deployable systems, compact semiconductor laser platforms combining ultra-narrow linewidth, fast frequency control, low SWaP, and broad wavelength accessibility are expected to play an increasingly important role.
